utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and outside. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please take your earphones. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom. I would like that you have God's peace, and I hope that this trial would conclude with divine providence. And I greet the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last time, Mr. Witness, we left off on document 1D168.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the document admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the topic discussed at that time was an exchange, all for all. You said at the time that Mr. Begovic [as interpreted] sent a letter to representatives in July, which is document 1D68 [as interpreted], containing his plan of the evacuation of, if possible, the entire population of Zepa. And on pages -- on the page 3233, lines 18 to 19, you gave an answer: "I don't think that his plan was implemented." Do you remember having answered my question in that manner? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we discussed it, but I don't remember exactly the words I used.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, since the witness cannot recollect, can we please have 1D68 [as interpreted] on our screens? Yes, it's up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I would kindly ask the witness to look at page 3233, lines 18 to 19, and I'm citing: "This has not been implemented according to his plan because the BS had evacuated the Zepa population." Does that help with your recollection, and is that the answer that you gave me? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure it's the answer I gave you, but, yes, the evacuation of Zepa, I was not aware of a plan by Izetbegovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Begovic"] until I got here for this trial, so my understanding at the time was that the Serbs and UNPROFOR had agreed to evacuate people from Zepa into Bosniak territory, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, was that an agreement between UNPROFOR and the Army of the RS, without the consent of the Zepa Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I know that the Zepa Muslims, as you called them, had agreed -- had signed a document of agreement with the VRS, against General Smith's better advice, but eventually, regardless of the detail of that agreement, the VRS was there, UNPROFOR had deployed more troops to Zepa to prevent something like Srebrenica from happening, and it was agreed to evacuate everyone as quickly as possible under UNPROFOR supervision, but with Serb-provided buses and trucks and fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you, if you were talking about Mr. Izetbegovic or Begovic, as we called it in page 2, line 23?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as shown on the letter, it's Izetbegovic, the president, and I think that's the name that should have appeared on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the document will be received, as required by the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D168 will be Exhibit D54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please now have in e-court document 1D168 -- correction, 1D68 [as interpreted]. I apologise. Thank you. It's a review of a document compiled by Viktor Bezruchenko, a lieutenant-colonel and a member of the command of the sector, just like Mr. Otin [as interpreted] was. It's entitled "The Fall of Zepa, The Review of Military Developments." We're going to look at this document, and can we please see in e-court the English version of the document. I repeat the number. It's 1D186, 1D186, page 27 in English, paragraph 101. And in the Serbian language, it's page 27 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Just some clarification for the record. We've got some uncertainty in the transcript. General Tolimir referred to Mr. Bezruchenko as a member of the command, and then there was a reference to another individual, and now it's disappeared. I think he said -- or at least what I heard was he was a lieutenant-colonel and a member of the command, just like somebody, and then there was a caret in the transcript and now it's all gone. I don't know if there was an actual part to the question that referred to another person, first of all, that needs to be reflected in the transcript; and, secondly, I'm not sure to which command General Tolimir is referring to in July of 1995. I think everybody's agreed that Mr. Bezruchenko was a member of the Civil Affairs Office of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, if you use e-court, you could go back to that portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to page 3 in my version, line 24. It's at the point where General Tolimir called out for the document 1D68. At one point, he referred to another individual in addition to Mr. Bezruchenko. It's no longer there. I just didn't know whether we -- or he wants a reference to this other individual that he mentioned. It's disappeared from the transcript, so unfortunately looking at the transcript is not going to help us at the moment, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will help us. I would like to clarify the situation and to quote on page 3, line 24. Mr. Tolimir said: "It's a review of a document compiled by Viktor Bezruchenko, a lieutenant-colonel and a member of the command, entitled "The Fall of Zepa, The Review of Military Developments." And you're referring to this portion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As I said, when the question was first asked, there was a reference to another individual and that has disappeared from the transcript, so I just wanted to make sure that it was reflecting General Tolimir's question properly. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're now satisfied with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm satisfied. I don't know whether, for his purposes, General Tolimir is satisfied with this individual having disappeared from the transcript. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, would you like to comment on the comment of Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I said that Bezruchenko was a member of the command, and the French lieutenant-general. It is correct what Mr. Thayer said, that he was in charge of Civil Affairs, but I said that he was also the lieutenant-colonel like Mr. Louis Fortin. I think that was the name that Mr. Thayer was looking for. He had the same rank like Louis Fortin, and probably the interpreters didn't hear me because I speak too fast and not as properly as should be required for the interpreters to manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you sure that you said it's a French lieutenant-general?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that I said he was a Frenchman. He was a member of the command of the UNPROFOR French contingent in charge of civil affairs. Probably, according to his name, he might be of the Ukrainian descent, or maybe something else. I'm not sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we should continue the examination of the witness. Would you like to put a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we have on our screens page 27, paragraph 101, and in the B/C/S it's also page 27. I'm interested in the first sentence under 101, which reads: "President Izetbegovic, on the 25th of July, in his letter to the Security Council, requested UNPROFOR to assist with the safe evacuation of the civilians. The Security Council immediately responded through a presidential statement in the positive way." And we can see that there was proof of what is written here. My question for the witness was whether you were aware and whether it was general knowledge at the time that the command of UNPROFOR and your sector knew that Izetbegovic addressed the Security Council, asking UNPROFOR to facilitate with the evacuation, and the Security Council issued a presidential statement granting this request.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being aware of discussions at that level. As you see, discussions are happening between President Izetbegovic and General Smith. I may have been aware of that information being passed on to General Gobillard, and I usually was with him when he met General Smith, so I may have been aware that this had been requested. But on the 25th of July, I was just about to leave for Zepa, so it's possible that I was not made aware of that information. But I don't recall for sure, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I would kindly ask you to respond to my question, which is: Did your command and UNPROFOR know that Alija Izetbegovic had written a letter to the Security Council with regard to the evacuation of the population from Zepa, and that the Security Council had confirmed that through a presidential statement of theirs?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first question he asked me if I knew, and as I said, I don't recall for sure. Now, that UNPROFOR knew, probably, but I'm assuming. I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Whenever the Security Council issued such a presidential statement according to Bezruchenko, did that impose any obligations on UNPROFOR, and did such statements have any reflection on the way UNPROFOR was bound to act? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if such an agreement came from the Security Council, of course, UNPROFOR would have to do its best to execute. If any orders coming from such high up -- or agreements were beyond UNPROFOR's ability, then again it would be UNPROFOR's duty to report back and say, Well, in order to execute, we need more time, more resources, or we suggest a different approach. But generally we would -- UNPROFOR would obey directives coming from the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the presidential statement of the Security Council a directive that should have been perceived as such by UNPROFOR commanders?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We'd have to look at the document, and all that I have is a statement -- I believe it's a statement by Mr. Bezruchenko which refers to that. I can't assume from a third document that this order is what you say it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The document he references to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the accused please read the numbers slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can pull up this document, show it to you, and perhaps ask those who were charged with implementing the decisions of the Security Council. Let me remind you. On page of the transcript 3233 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document number is N043043531. Thank you. Based on this document, one can see that the Security Council had issued a presidential statement. Thank you. This is not in e-court. It's only mentioned in the footnote referenced by Mr. Bezruchenko. Therefore, I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, you said, on page 3233, line 19, that the VRS had evacuated the population. Is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, when I arrived on the 26th of July, as I recounted last Thursday, it had already started. Buses and trucks were used, with usually a Ukrainian soldier on board, to make sure that the Bosniak population of Zepa was sent to where it was intended to be sent, so yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now see in e-court page 25 of the report that we are seeing currently on our screens. That's 1D186, page 29, paragraph 105, which reads as follows, and I quote -- it's the next page in English: "UNPROFOR started evacuation from Zepa on 25 July. French Battalion 2 of Sector Sarajevo, in the afternoon of the 25th July, sent a medivac convoy to Zepa for evacuation of the wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, can you look at this portion in your language as well? Thank you. My question is: Is this contradictory to what you say, that the VRS was the one who commenced the evacuation from Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's contradictory. And who started in what order, I don't recall for sure. But as we see the next line, a thousand people were evacuated using VRS buses, so in my mind - I was on the road at the time - it's part of one big operation which is co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the first evacuation was conducted by using the vehicles of your command and UNPROFOR and that 151 wounded or sick people were evacuated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the text in front of me says, and I have no reason to doubt its validity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Can we please now see document -- page 23 of Bezruchenko's description of the events, which is document 1D186 that we are currently seeing on our screens. It's page 26, paragraph 86, in the Serbian language, through to 89. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Will you please look at item 86, the last paragraph, which reads: "The Defence of Zepa has collapsed, and surrender of the enclave to the BSA has been accepted. Large numbers of DPs wishing to seek refuge in federation-controlled territory will therefore have to be moved." UNPROFOR, in its operative order dated 20th of July, assessed the situation in this manner as I just read out to you. So I'm talking about a report from the operative order issued by the UNPROFOR. Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect -- I did not recollect it in those exact words, but, yes, it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that an operative order of UNPROFOR that was compiled already on the 20th of July; do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see the document that is referenced, but there's no -- there's no date. It says [indiscernible] "11/95." I'll have to look at the document, itself, on the date. But paragraph 86 says it is dated 20th of July, so, again, I have no reason to doubt that that information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Could you please tell me whether UNPROFOR had its own tasks within that order in relation to Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall that order by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to remind you. Bezruchenko says, I quote: "UNPROFOR should, together with the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the UNHCR and the International Red Cross, co-ordinate the relocation of displaced persons to Zenica. The evacuation was supposed to take place in three stages, and it was supposed to involve UNPROFOR forces from Sector Sarajevo, Sector North-East, Sector South-West, as well as the UNPROFOR Command. The Command of the Drina Corps in that stage co-ordinated practical preparations for the evacuation of people from Zepa." That is what Mr. Bezruchenko says. I have reminded you of that, what the plan contains, and now I'm going to ask you the following: Do we see from this report of Bezruchenko's that even before the 24th of July, before Alija Izetbegovic spoke to the Security Council on the 25th of July, the UNPROFOR -- or, rather, UNPROFOR issued this order that Bezruchenko is referring to and that has to do with evacuation. Can you explain to us who was in charge of issuing this kind of order within UNPROFOR before all of these things happened? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who the person would be, but it's operations at headquarters UNPROFOR who would issue that kind of order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Could I please have the statement of this witness, that is, D50, and could we see page 20, paragraph 4 in Serbian. In English, it's page 21 and the last paragraph at that. Thank you. The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that paragraph, where it says -- we see the fourth paragraph, don't we, on both sides: "Gobillard later found out that Smith and Karl Bildt had recently met with Mladic, and Smith was told by Mladic that Zepa was in his hands. Smith then went to Izetbegovic to discuss UNPROFOR assistance in the evacuation of the population." And now my question: In relation to the evacuation of the sick and wounded from Zepa, did UNPROFOR do that before or after this meeting of Mr. Smith's? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was done after. The previous document, we were looking at July 25th for the evacuation of the injured and sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And on what date was the operative order issued in relation to these documents, I mean, in terms of this military analysis that Bezruchenko is referring to? Do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Bezruchenko's statement, it was July 20th, but such an operation order is not necessarily the only one issued on a certain subject. For example, in most of the countries they used a NATO system. You issue an operation order, and then as the situation evolves, you issue supplementary order to that operational order to take into account changes in the situation, evolution in the situation, resources that you counted on that are no longer available, and so forth. But as I said, the order -- the initial order was dated July 20th, according to Bezruchenko's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the part we quoted just now, the sentence stating: "Gobillard later found out that Smith and Karl Bildt had recently met with Mladic," does that perhaps pertain to the 19th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have page 30, paragraph 106. Thank you. Again, it is this report of Viktor Bezruchenko's. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 106, paragraph 106, both in Serbian and in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have the appropriate English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo report for the 26th of July described the situation as follows: "In accordance with the order of UNPROFOR commander and decision of sector commander, our units took part in the evacuation of wounded people from Zepa to Sarajevo and civil population to Kladanj. This process is ongoing." Then it goes on, I quote: "UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo G2 office assessed that Zepa looks like under BSA control one way or another." "G2 also noted there was no UNHCR or ICRC representatives on the ground and that General Tolimir respected the evacuation agreement, and that the BSA apparently were seeking to complete the evacuation on the 26th of July." In relation to this citation, I have a few questions. There's a reference to the commander of UNPROFOR and the sector commander and their reports -- or, rather, their orders. Do you know whether there was this kind of order issued by the two commanders, and do you know who was the commander of UNPROFOR at the time and who was the commander of Sector Sarajevo in charge of Zepa at the time? Do you remember? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already talked about the order. The sector commander at the time was General Gobillard and the UNPROFOR commander was General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw, in this paragraph, that Bezruchenko is conveying that Tolimir respected the evacuation agreement and the BSA apparently was seeking to complete the evacuation on the 26th of July. My question is as follows: Can you explain, in situations when the civilian population is evacuated, how important is it for it to be carried out quickly and efficiently in war zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think "quickly" is not the key word here, but "efficiently" is. As I mentioned the other day, it's important that on the receiving end that the government and local authorities are prepared to take in an imported influx of people, people coming with nothing, basically, so they need to be looked after in every respect. So efficiently for that purpose and also for the purpose of ensuring that everybody gets to where they're supposed to go under UNPROFOR escort, which was UNPROFOR's part in that evacuation, escorting every vehicle, having one soldier on board every vehicle, to make sure that they were going to their destination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fortin. I would like to ask the President for the document 1D186 to admit -- to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, first I would like to see the first page to identify the document, and I would like to know how many pages this document contains.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you are putting this question, my legal advisor is checking how many pages the document contains. The document has been translated both into Serbian and English, and we received it from the database. I have just found out from my legal advisor that the document has 35 pages and that it was translated both into English and Serbian, and it speaks of the chronology of what happened in Srebrenica -- sorry, I do apologise, in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to provide the Trial Chamber with some context to the document. I think the Trial Chamber probably has a sense that on our side, our approach to evidence coming before the Trial Chamber is the more the merrier. In this case, what this is is a narrative that was drafted by Mr. Bezruchenko, who is a military analyst employed by the OTP. At the time, as we've already heard, he was a Civil Affairs officer with UNPROFOR. This narrative was drafted at a late date in the Popovic trial and, therefore, was not relied upon by the Prosecution at all in that case, nor do we intend to rely upon the report or Mr. Bezruchenko's testimony in this case as well. We have other witnesses who testified in Popovic. So this is somewhat akin, I suppose, to an expert report, although we have never relied on it, we don't intend to rely on it. We've got all the live witnesses and the documents already on our witness list who will testify and provide their accounts and authenticate documents first-hand. So there's probably a lot in this narrative that will never see the light of day one way or the other. We've got no problem with that, but I just wanted the Trial Chamber to understand that this is not -- as opposed to, for example, an expert report by Richard Butler, who will be coming to testify, will not be returned to by the Prosecution over and over again. Just to give you that sense of background to the document. Again, we've got no objection to it coming in before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the whole document or only those parts -- those paragraphs used in examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like the entire document to be admitted into evidence. As you have heard, the document was compiled in a certain way. There's no need for me to repeat it. I would like to ask for it to be admitted in its entirety. If necessary, if you give me enough time, I can put questions in relation to the entire document, but I selected just a few so that I could put more questions in relation to other things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The entire document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have in e-court D50. That is his statement. Page 22 of that statement - thank you - in Serbian, that is. It's page 24 in English. Thank you. Thank you. Now we see page 22 and 24. 24 is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now we are briefly going to deal with the question of the agreement. You witnessed the signing of that agreement. The question was whether the agreement on the exchange of all for all -- I'm actually referring to page 24 and paragraph number 2. It says here: "Smith told us that the agreement had just been signed without the authority of the Bosnian government." And now again you say: "However, even though Smith had told them and confirmed that no such agreement had been signed, they believed it had happened." On the basis of these two matters, when talking to the representatives of the Muslims, did you find out how come they had grounds to believe that the agreement on the exchange of prisoners, all for all, had been signed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the -- that these two representatives knew that there was an agreement all for all, because there was no such agreement, and General Smith was telling them not to sign that agreement with Mladic because an all-for-all prisoner exchange agreement did not exist. And as we discussed last week, UNPROFOR could not provide all the guarantees that this agreement was proposing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Could 1D163 -- that is to say, 1D163, could we have that in e-court, page 2, the first paragraph, lines 1 through 11. That's a document of two pages. I assume that it has two pages in English as well. So page 2. Thank you, we see the first page. The date is the 20th of July, 1995. That was on the first page, and now I am reading out the following. It's the penultimate paragraph: "The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this point in time has a total of 350 aggressor soldiers in our prisons. The agreement all for all that was reached on the 20th of July at the airport means that all members of the army from all aggressor prisons and camps, including those in Srebrenica, should be released, as well as the entire population," or, rather --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you, because you were reading too fast and the last portion of this quotation was not translated. Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for having cautioned me. I'm going to read the last sentence slowly for the benefit of the interpreters: "Our request is for the completion of the evacuation, first of all, of the civilian population from Zepa in the first phase, followed then by those fit for military service as you requested." This is what I'd like to point out, "as you requested," in the way in which you had requested: "The all-for-all agreement, well done. We would be grateful if you can pull it off. That is the response from Zepa. If you save the people from Zepa, they and the combatants will be eternally grateful. Please inform us tomorrow following the negotiations about them. Over." Could we now please look at page 1 of this agreement, both in Serbian and in English, so that we would see that it was written on the 20th and that it is a government official that is presenting this, Amor Masovic, who was in charge of prisoner exchanges in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question for Mr. Fortin would be as follows: Did he know that the Muslims already had Amor Masovic's report on the all-for-all exchange already on the 20th and that that is why they said that they believed that the agreement had been signed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I don't know who this Masovic is. And on the second page, the following paragraph was alluding to "inform us tomorrow on the results," so perhaps it was not an agreement that was signed. Perhaps it was just a document that was being discussed. So I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. I have clearly read this out to you, and now we're going to add the following. We're actually going to see where the agreement was signed. Amor Masovic says this. I have just read out the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, 1D167, could that be displayed, please. Thank you. We see it in Serbian. Could it please be shown to the witness in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we see the document. This is a report from the 26th of July. It's a report from Zepa that, and I quote: "Mr. President, minister, the negotiations at Boksanica ended this evening. They were attended by General Smith, and the criminal Mladic," that's what he says, "and Hamdija Torlak, the chairman of Zepa Municipality Executive Committee. Nothing was agreed at these negotiations because General Smith did not bring the agreement on the all-for-all exchange, but today I was informed by the General Staff that the agreement on this all-for-all exchange had been accepted by our side and that General Smith had taken it with him. General Smith stated in the presence of Hamdija Torlak that you were seeking a few more concessions for the exchange to take place. "If this has not been resolved by them by 8.00, the negotiations will be ended and UNPROFOR will withdraw from Zepa." Mr. Fortin, can one see, on the basis of this document, that the Muslims from Zepa, their War Presidency, are informing Alija Izetbegovic about the fact that they knew that an all-for-all agreement had been signed, and we saw that Amor Masovic had told them as far back as the 20th that an all-for-all agreement had been signed, and that he gave them the exact order or sequence in which it was to be carried out? Can you not see that this was well known even before General Smith came? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, because towards the bottom third of that same letter, he asks Izetbegovic: "We ask you once again if you have accepted and signed the all-for-all agreement, please send it overnight to General Smith ..." "If you have accepted and signed the all-for-all agreement." In the previous letter where you showed that discussion had happened on the 20th of July, there was a sentence that I had time to read which said that discussions were to carry on the next day at 11.00 with Mr. Bulajic, who was the representative of the Serbs for the Prisoner Exchange Commission, I guess, and was not present on the 20th, so that does not prove anything. That does not prove that the agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. I'm sorry, you can finish what you have started to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, we are looking at a document with a date 26th of July, 1995, and you should continue your answer, Mr. Fortin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that does not prove that the -- that there was an all-for-all agreement on prisoner exchange as early as the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Can I please have document 1D167 entered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D56.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to the document that we had seen a short while ago, which is 1D163, page 2. This is a telegram sent by Amor Masovic to the Bosnian leadership in Zepa. Thank you. Can we please look at line 3 on page 2 in the B/C/S, and it's in paragraph 2 on page 2 in the English, which reads: "The all-for-all agreement reached at the airport on the 20th of July includes the release of all members of the army from all of the aggressor's prisons and camps, including the new captives from Srebrenica ..." I'm not going to read this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All I wanted to ask you is this: This representative of the Army of BH for exchange of prisoners, is he talking about an agreement that had been reached on the 20th of July and that it implied an exchange of prisoners all for all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would kindly ask the President for document 1D163 to be admitted into evidence, provided it's not already been admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe in the interests of saving a little bit of redirect examination time, while we have this document on the screen, and we have no objection to its admission, if we could just look at page 1 of the document. And we've spent some time on this document. Again just to save some time, General Tolimir has repeatedly referred to this as evidence of a signed agreement, and I just ask if the witness could be given an opportunity to read the first paragraph of this document, and that way I don't have to call it up again and deal with it in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, do you have any additional question to the witness on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions relating to this document. All I want is that now we see 1D164, dated the 19th, be shown in this courtroom, which shows the follow-up and the continuity of the signing of the agreement on exchange all for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next document, I would like to ask the witness if he could comment on the first paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. In the middle of the first paragraph, this is the little paragraph that I said I had time to read: "Since the aggressor's commission did not include their representative from the Commission for Exchange, Dragan Bulajic, the details of the agreement could not be hammered out, the number of persons to be exchanged on both sides, but both sides agreed to continue the negotiations at 1100 hours tomorrow." So the following paragraph on page 2 does not refer to an agreement reached and signed on the 20th, as we can see there in that same document, and that's the point I was making earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we should proceed to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Fortin, if two commissions reach an agreement and they do not enter each and every name of the persons subject of this agreement, should those who are subsequently to implement this agreement obliged to add any names that would be subject of the exchange?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with this type of a negotiation and I was not privy to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at this document that we see now in front of us, which is 1D164. Can we please enlarge it so that we can read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that this document was received by the Communications Centre in Sarajevo, that it was addressed to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, Prime Minister Silajdzic, president of the association of the people from Zepa, Bahir Helic [phoen]. We see that this was sent by the War Presidency of Zepa. We can see that that on page 2. And it was signed by the commander of the 285th Light Zepa Brigade, and it reads as follows: "On 19th July, there was a meeting between the representatives of the civilian authorities of Zepa municipality, attended by Hamdija Torlak and Hamdija Kulovac, and the representatives of the Chetnik side, Generals Mladic and Tolimir, and the chief of the Ukrainian Company. "The Serbian side set the following conditions ..." Under A, sub-item A, to exchange the wounded according to the following schedule. I'm reading item 1: "Safe passage should be allowed across the Serbian territory by free choice to the population according to the following schedule:" And I repeat "free choice." "A. The wounded and the sick. "B. Women and small children." And the remainder of the population. After that: "Transportation from Zepa would be provided from Zepa by using the vehicles of the aggressor's side and with an UNPROFOR escort both at the front and the rear of the convoy. That mode would be applied to the first three categories mentioned under item 1." And so on and so forth. I'm not going to read the whole document. In your opinion, and please look at page 2 as well, was this document signed by the Zepa War Presidency and the commander of Zepa, and did this document reach Sarajevo, as you can see from the addressee and the time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read a little. So your question, the document signed -- was this document signed by the Zepa War Presidency and the commander of Zepa, so the commander of the 285th Light Brigade, and did it reach Sarajevo? I don't know if it reached Sarajevo, but it seems to have been drafted by those two individuals you mention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry for the intervention again. I just want the record to be clear. When General Tolimir read out from this document, and I'm referring to page 25, line 15, he said that under A, sub-item A: "To exchange the wounded according to the following schedule." I just want the record to reflect correctly that there is no reference in this passage that he read to any exchange. This document clearly, on its face, simply refers to the conditions that were set by Generals Mladic and Tolimir at this meeting with the local Zepa representatives on 19 July for the removal of the civilian population from Zepa, and it had nothing to do with exchange, if we look at the language itself. That was inserted by General Tolimir, and I want the record to be clean and clear on that count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said "passage," not "exchange," but I'm grateful to Mr. Thayer if the transcript was wrong. I would like to have this document, 1D164, admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the discussion, the specific line is, I quote: "The Serbian side set the following conditions ..." The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D58.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. While we still have this document on the screen, can we please look at page 2 in order to clarify what Mr. Thayer was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at item 5, second paragraph, which reads: "The Muslims of Zepa, the War Presidency and the commander, they say: "We urgently ask the government to do the following: "A. To provide 400 of the aggressor's soldiers for exchange from the list held by Amor Masovic. "B. To provide transportation by helicopter for all categories of the population, except for the wounded, sick, and the elderly." My question is: Based on this report, can one conclude that the Serbian Army accepted, but that the Muslims were asking their government to do this, not Mladic and Tolimir? This was the request that the Muslims posed to their government with respect to providing transportation by helicopter and other requests; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the letter seems to first relay what you, General Tolimir, and Mladic offered, and, second, to ask that it be accepted by the government to ensure the fate of the people of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But tell us this : In this report, did the Army of Republika Srpska accept the exchange of all the Zepa Brigade soldiers and that they be transported by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's the War Presidency of Zepa municipality and the commander of the 285th Brigade that add that paragraph B and D or paragraph -- yeah, B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have this document, 1D164, into evidence. However, since it's already in evidence, let's move to a next document to see what initiatives were undertaken by whom. In that regard, can we please see document 1D165. Thank you. While we are waiting for the document to appear, it is my duty to say that this particular document was drafted back on the 13th of July and that it was sent, as you can see, on 10.30 on the 13th of July from Zepa to Sarajevo in order to prove that the document was dispatched by the encrypting officer. The commander was Rasim Delic, and he confirmed it was Zepa who had requested negotiations with the VRS and not the other way 'round. So look at this document. It was drafted on the 13th of July and was dispatched -- or, rather, received by the General Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina at 10.30. It says: "We received a report at 0920 hours through our communications system that people have rallied in Zepa demanding that the president of the War Presidency attend negotiations with the Chetniks, not to agree to do anything at these negotiations, but rather prolong the whole process in order to achieve something resolved on the international stage." So the president of the War Presidency is asking for the attendance of the negotiations to be postponed. The second paragraph reads: "We reported your view that there should be no negotiations and that Zepa should be helped militarily and politically." Thank you. My question is: Can one see from this document that the population of Zepa had been asking for negotiations way back on the 13th, but that the member of the Presidency of the Republic of BH did not grant that request and that he conveyed the views of the president, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The prime minister, Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it seemed that Delic is requesting a clarification. Zepa wants to negotiate. Apparently, Silajdzic has said that, You can attend negotiation, but don't agree to anything. So it seems to me that Zepa, as early as the 13th of July, wanted to negotiate because they knew what happened in Srebrenica, but the Bosniak authorities were not too sure to let them negotiate at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at line 4 in English, where Rasim Delic is citing the reasons for not granting the request, and he says this: "... to prolong the negotiations, pending a resolution on the international stage." Was that the main reason for the Muslim authorities and the army not to prove these negotiations way back on the 13th of July, because they had anticipated that something would be resolved in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Tolimir, you're asking a major of UNPROFOR if the Muslim authority -- if it was their reason. All I can say is I'm reading the same letter as you do, sir, and I can't go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'm just wondering what the basis is of the General's assertion repeatedly that it was the Muslims that initiated the request for negotiations. We're all reading the same document, and unless there's some other document that General Tolimir is referring to to build in this repeated claim that the Muslims initiated the request for negotiation, I don't see it, and I'm wondering if there is a basis. And if there is, maybe that can be put to the witness so that we have a more helpful answer. But as it is, we're just looking at a document which we all can read, and Colonel Fortin has answered, I think, as fully as he can on this count. We're not going to get any further unless there's a further basis laid for General Tolimir's claim that it was the Zepa population which reached out to the VRS, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you clarify this question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer, for asking me to clarify. The population of Zepa, as one can see from this cable, wanted an evacuation way back on the 13th. However, Rasim Delic, as I read out in line 4, said, and I quote: "... to prolong the time in anticipation of a solution found on the international plane." Because in the previous transcript, it was not clear, and I now repeat, "on the international plane." My question was: Was that the reason to postpone the evacuation of the Zepa population, due to the fact that they were waiting for international support and assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered this question; that he personally doesn't know the motives of the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For that purpose, I kindly ask you to admit 1D165 into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D59.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I please now have in e-court P123, P123. Thank you. Here it is on our screens. It's a telegram that I sent from Zepa, and it reads, and I quote -- it's dated the 13th, and it confirms what was said, and I'm quoting: "In the afternoon, we did not expect the planned contact with representatives from Zepa, Torlak and Omanovic, as has been scheduled for us to meet at around 2100 hours." Second paragraph: "They informed us through UNPROFOR that they were active during the day in terms of informing the population about the conditions for the evacuation from Zepa, and that they were forced to do that because of the government decision in Sarajevo for them not to evacuate."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Mr. Fortin, from this document can one see that the Muslims failed to appear at the negotiations because the Muslim side was opposed to their request for negotiations, the fact that Mr. Silajdzic passed on to President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document that you drafted yourself, as you pointed out, says exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. It is true that I drafted it myself, and it is also true that that was the reason for my being in Zepa, because they were looking for a negotiator.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform you that this document was admitted into evidence by the Prosecution. It bears their number. And I would kindly ask the Chamber to have this document admitted into evidence, unless it's already been admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. As you see from the number, it is a document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 1D165 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you move to -- this is, I think, D59 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is perhaps the right time for the first break for today. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have the first break now, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, I apologise to the interpreters, because my legal advisors have warned me that I have really been speaking too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Fortin, could we now have a look at document 1D166 in e-court. 1D166. Now we see it. This is a continuation of the conversation that I asked about a few moments ago; that is, that Delic asked for international support. Now we see his report. Delic sent it to the Presidency of the Republic in Sarajevo. You can see on the stamp that it was received by the Presidency through the Communications Centre and that it was recorded on the 17th of July, 1995. I quote paragraph 1: "I have just finished talking to General Smith." That is to say, on the 18th: "Perhaps I could have women, children and the elderly from Zepa evacuated by UNPROFOR. Would you accept this?" Second: "Perhaps in this case we could insert a brigade (or a battalion) of soldiers to Zepa across the forest-path and thus continue combat with more success. These men from Zepa say that they could find between 500 and 1.000 volunteers (Muderis is from Zepa)." Paragraph 3: "Groups should also be inserted into Gorazde. This would be a great encouragement. There are people interested. "An evacuation plan for the population of Zepa has been made here in case items 1 and 2 above fail. I am sending it to you. "I am waiting for your answers to the above." Thank you. My question is as follows: Do you know whether on the 18th General Delic asked Smith to provide UNPROFOR assistance, and did Smith familiarise you, the sector command, because it had to do with Zepa, that was within your area of responsibility? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of who General Smith talked to regularly, but we at sector were aware that he was talking with the various parties continuously. So, yes, it's possible that on the 18th he had a conversation with -- with Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one see from these conversations that the Muslim side was actually putting off the evacuation, the negotiations, et cetera, and that they wanted to resolve the problem in Zepa through combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, there are two -- two issues here. There's the issue of the population, women, children, elderly, which they wanted evacuated, and the issue of the light brigade or the remnants of Bosniak forces in Zepa. And, yes, as we discussed last week, those -- those pockets were a nuisance to the Serbs, who wanted to get rid of them because their forces were spread out all over, and the Bosniaks wanted to maintain them, so that the VRS did not -- could not - how shall I say? - free the forces looking after those pockets and concentrate on Sarajevo, for example. So, yes, they were military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Since you said, in response to my question, that the Bosnian side minded the existence of this enclave, I would like us to see once again in e-court document 1D186. That is the document compiled by Mr. Bezruchenko in terms of military developments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D55.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before we move on to the question, could this document please be admitted into evidence, the one that we looked at a few moments ago, the communication between General Delic and the Presidency; that is to say, the gentleman who spoke to General Smith? 1D166, I would like to tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, I would like to ask the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Because of this answer, we have to go back once again to the causes of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Fortin, I would like to ask you to look at paragraph 3 of this report. Could you please see who it was that first started the conflict in Zepa? I quote: "On the 4th of June, 1992, a military convoy under the command of Major Dragan Suka moved from Pale to Zepa to relieve the JNA garrison. The convoy was ambushed by local Green Berets and the Patriotic League on the way to Zepa. In the ensuing fighting, the VRS sustained heavy casualties, including 45 soldiers killed and 31 wounded. The JNA garrison in Zepa was wiped out too. The operation was a defeat for the Bosnian Serbs." And so on and so forth, end of quotation. Please, do you know how far away the Zepa Garrison was from the Command of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it more than 100 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Where was the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the VRS was at Veliki Zep, in the area that had Muslim forces, the ones that we are talking about just now, only 10 kilometres away. So you see now how conflicts in this enclave broke out.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear -- I hear what you tell me, but, no, I don't see that this was the start. Perhaps it was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I gave you a document that presented military developments. Now I would like to remind you of some other documents that speak about that; namely, who needed Zepa more, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Army of Republika Srpska, who needed it more as an enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could we now display in e-court 1D777. I repeat, 1D177. I misspoke a moment ago when I was asking for the document. Thank you. Now we see the document, both in English and in Serbian. This is an order of the Command of the 28th Division in which it says, in paragraph 3, I quote: "The Division Command ordered its units to carry out certain combat tasks in the Srebrenica-Zepa corridor in order number 01-33/95 of the 17th of May, 1995. According to this order, the 282nd," and so on, "Brigade are to carry out daily reconnaissance and patrol activities in the corridor in order to protect the corridor from being intersected by the aggressor. This will be carried out by armed patrols," et cetera, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is as follows: This document dates back to May 1995, and does it not show that Srebrenica is maintaining this corridor with Zepa, which is why these two enclaves were separated, because the Muslims had been using that corridor for arming? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the document does show that there was a corridor in between Zepa and Srebrenica. But, personally, that's not something that I was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Now you have seen that as far back as May, this activity was resorted to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 1D179, please. 1D179, could it please be displayed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the document 1D177?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Precisely. I have just forgotten to say that. Thank you for having reminded me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. At page 38, lines 7 and 8, in the question from General Tolimir, you say: "Yes, the document shows that there was a corridor between Zepa and Srebrenica." Although you personally were not familiar with this, are you in a position to explain the composition of this corridor, who was maintaining it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, like I said, ma'am, I'm not familiar with that corridor because we -- I was at sector level, Sector Sarajevo. We were responsible for Zepa, but not for Srebrenica, so -- and we had limited number of observation posts around Zepa. They may have been reporting that there was a Bosnian activity link, a corridor between the two enclaves, but I was not familiar with that. Our attention came -- focused on Zepa in mid-July when the activities -- military activities by the VRS started happening in that area. But that's not surprising that the Bosnians would maintain a corridor between two isolated enclaves as long as they were able to do so, but I don't know the details of the nature of military operations, the nature of equipment or supplies or information that was transported through that corridor. But it's not surprising that it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Judge Nyambe. Thank you, Mr. Fortin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Fortin, could you please say whether there were any protests in Zepa, any protests of the population, because -- rather, in Srebrenica, because the UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, where DutchBat was, had placed a check-point near that corridor precisely in the month of May, and did the Muslims ask for this check-point to be removed? Thank you. Do you know anything about that? If you don't, we're going to deal with it with other witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We now see before us a document. I'm going to read something out now, and then I'm going to put a question to you. First of all, I'm going to tell you that this order was written by the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Corps, Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic, and he says -- this is an order from the month of June, that is to say, a month before these events that we are speaking of. This is what he is ordering: "1. Execute all preparations in the Command of the 28th --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have dealt with this document already last week and the witness has seen it. I think it's not necessary to read it again for the record. We have it as a document. Just put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From this document, can it be seen that the Muslim side had been involved in active operations conducted from the protected area of Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does show -- it does show that they were planning to fight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at document 1D181 now. Thank you. This is document 1D181. Please look at paragraph 6, which is on the next page in English. So let's look at paragraph 3. It reads in English as follows: "About 40 Chetniks were killed and dozens were wounded. A significant quantity of infantry weapons were seized ..." In brackets, they specify exactly what. "One aggressor soldier was also lightly wounded in the chest, and he was captured in Vrani Kamen area." His name was Velimir Mrdjan, born in 1975, in Glamoc, and so on and so forth. In paragraph 3 of this same document, it says that as reported by this command, an order was issued to set up a number of sabotage groups to be sent deep into the temporarily controlled area, with a view to inflicting losses on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that we don't know exactly which paragraph is being cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Since a moment ago Judge Nyambe asked you about the corridor, and we also saw an order for the Muslims to become combat operations in June, now we have a report from Zepa stating that 40 members of the VRS were killed in that period. Can we please scroll the document down to see its provenance. You see that it comes from the 285th Light Brigade of Zepa, and that was a month prior to the activities that we were discussing. This report says that the author had killed 40 Serbs in Srebrenica before any activities were started. Is UNPROFOR aware of any protests from the VRS to the effect that active combat operations had been conducted from Zepa and that Zepa actually had not been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As discussed last week, we were aware at UNPROFOR that there had been raids conducted from -- by the Bosnians from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa into Serb-held territory. I, personally, did not know the details, but I remembered them, I remembered them. But this only shows that war was still on, regardless of UNPROFOR's presence. Both parties were willing to keep fighting. The next page of the document that's on e-court right now shows the same person talking, saying that they were shelled on the 27th of June, so war was still on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fortin. Can we please now look at document 1D180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering this document, 1D179? Sorry, 1D181. 1D181.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D62.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now have document 1D182 now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D52.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now see document 1D182. Thank you. Thank you. We can see the document issued by the Command of the 2nd Corps, confirming what had been reported by Mr. Palic, as we've seen a minute ago. In the second paragraph, it says: "Sixty Chetniks were liquidated, and according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Given that you said that combat operations were still underway, can one discern from this document that before the negotiations started in Zepa on the 8th of July, the corps command informed the units about how successful the Zepa Brigade was, and does this show that it was involved in combat operations launched from a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this shows that the Bosnians were preparing and willing to fight. And, Mr. President, the first paragraph in that document is interesting, in that it summarises an issue that we've been coming back to from every angle for close to two days now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. All I wanted to say was to point out to you that this document was reached by the corps command and that it informed all the units that combat operations were conducted from the protected area. My question was whether the UNPROFOR command subordinated to your sector was familiar with the fact that the Muslims were conducting military operations from the protected zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, this is a repetition. We have heard the answer of the witness. You were dealing with this document earlier, and you should try to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please now see document 1D180. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at paragraph 2, line 4 in both versions, which reads that: "On the 16th of February, 1994 [as interpreted], the aggressor filed a request with UNPROFOR to declare Zepa a non-demilitarised zone with the following rationale." Bullet point 1: "BH Army helicopter flights supplying weapons and ammunition have been registered; "The movements of the BH Army have been noticed and registered in the Zepa sector; "Accusing members of the Ukrainian Battalion that they were covering up for the activities and intentions of the BH Army, which is why they no longer guarantee safety; "That on the night between the 15th and 16th February, our helicopters were seen flying over and that infantry fire was opened on them." Then in the next paragraph, under the first bullet point, we see, with reference to the 17th of February, it says that helicopter reconnaissance was scheduled to be conducted by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell me, do you remember this letter, and do you know whether it had reached your command HQ?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid we were not on the Bosnian distribution list for that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you see that even the Muslims from Sarajevo were informing the Muslims of Zepa that the VRS had filed a protest against the activities being conducted way back in February 1995? Can you infer that from the document written on the 17th of February, 1995, and submitted to the Command of the OG-8 Srebrenica and the 1st Zepa Brigade Command, and it was written by the Army General Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And I have quoted only certain portions of it.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it shows that the Muslims from Sarajevo were informing those of Zepa, and the only conclusion I draw from that is that the protests that the Serbs submitted was, in fact, acted upon by UNPROFOR. When one side protested, it was UNPROFOR's duty to bring it to the attention of the other side, which obviously was done in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just so there's absolutely no doubt about the Prosecution's position, the Prosecution, I think, has made it clear from day one that there is no dispute that there were military excursions conducted by the ABiH from inside the protected areas, resulting in military losses as well as civilian losses to the Serbs. There are adjudicated facts on this issue. It is something that is absolutely not in dispute. Indeed, the specific fact of helicopter resupply of weaponry to the Muslims in the enclaves is also something that is not in dispute by the Prosecution and, again, is an adjudicated fact. I don't know if this is going to help save some time, but it is not in contest in this case, as far as the Prosecution's concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I understand your comment to help Mr. Tolimir to shorten his examination and to leave this kind of -- this matter, and continue, perhaps, with another topic. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now let's look at document 1D129. I would like to ask the witness whether he knows anything about this document. Thank you. Thank you. We can see the first page on this document, entitled "Final Analysis of the Srebrenica and Zepa Air-Lift." It was drafted by the ABiH army, specifically the command of its anti-aircraft defence and air force. Can we please now look at page 2 of this document. Thank you. We can see page 2 in both languages, and in paragraph 2, after the title "Introduction," it says, and I quote: "Between the 27th February 1993 and 7th of May, 1995, there was an air-lift from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to meet the needs of the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde. The main aim of introducing and maintaining the air-lift was to transport and ensure combat equipment ..." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Was the Command of the Sarajevo Sector, which was in charge of the Zepa and Srebrenica safe havens, as well as the UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo, know that there was air-lift procedures providing weapons in the period between the 27th of February, 1993, and the 7th of May, 1995, as stated in this report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps UNPROFOR knew about it, but I didn't. I arrived on 15 May, and the document shows that this happened between February 1993 and 7 May 1995. And, unfortunately, the pace was quite hectic as soon as I arrived, and I didn't have time to go back and read about what had been happening since the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. I would like to ask you to look at page 7 of this document, paragraph B. It is actually 3(B). We see what it says there: "Number of hours of flight: 1025. "GMI fuel use, approximately 8.200 litres," that is to say, over 8 tonnes. "Transport to Zepa, 17 tonnes of lethal weapons." Do you see that, and do you see that this was functioning incessantly up until the 7th of May, up until you arrived, since you arrived in the beginning of May, and was that something that those whom you had succeeded knew about as well?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, they may well have known. I don't know if they did, and I did not know those details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Trial Chamber please admit this document into evidence. It contains the answer to the question that was put here when the witness was being examined. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness said: "They may well have known. I don't know if they did, and I did not know those details." Is this the right witness to tender this document or should you leave it for the time to deal with it with another witness who can say something about authenticity or the content?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender this into evidence as proof and that confirms what Judge Nyambe asked about, whether there was a corridor that was transporting weapons, et cetera. I'm presenting this as proof, and I therefore believe it can be admitted into evidence, because the witness is saying that he did not know, and UNPROFOR was in Zepa and they could have known. Thank you. Could it please be admitted? And now I'm going to show you a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. The Chamber will confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please have the first page of this document on the screen, and then the last page. Could we now see the page with the signature of the author.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The signature can be seen on the first page, where it says: "Colonel Erdin Hrustic, standing in for the commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We would like to ask the Prosecution on their position, tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will mark this document for identification so that it can be identified during the examination of other witnesses, because this witness is not in the position to tell us anything about the content and the source, where the document is coming from. And therefore it will only be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D129 will be marked for identification as Exhibit D63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we are not certain about this document yet, we are now going to move on to another group of questions. Could I please have 65 ter 0142. It is Prosecution 65 ter 0142. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, you should switch off your microphone when you have a private discussion. Please carry on now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My assistant just told me that we were supposed to show the bottom part of this page and the second page, because we could not see at first the part of the text that I wanted to have displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read out part of the text to you, and this document was written on the 12th of July. It was written by this accused person.
