This is what it says in the last paragraph: "The Muslims wish to present things as if Srebrenica had been demilitarised and that there was only civilian population in it. That is why --" Could we please move on to the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now we see what it says here. Yes, thank you. "Could all able-bodied persons of military age be ordered to illegally pull out from the area, cross RS territory, and reach Muslim-controlled territory so that they could accuse the VRS of having carried out an unprovoked attack on civilians in a safe haven." Thank you. Further on, it says: "Bearing in mind that it is very important to arrest as many members of the crushed Muslim units as possible, or liquidate them if they resist, it is equally important to register all the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari." "The OBP organs will brief the MUP organs in their respective zones of responsibility on the information received; they will draw up joint plans for breaking up and liquidating enemy formations trying to escape from the Srebrenica enclave towards Tuzla and Kladanj." Signature: "Major General Zdravko Tolimir." Thank you. My question would be as follows: Were the Muslims trying to represent things as follows: that both Zepa and Srebrenica were demilitarised zones where there were only civilians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you say in your text, General, but I don't believe so, since they were, you've shown earlier with previous documents, ordering troops in those enclaves to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was pressure exerted towards UNPROFOR to represent the enclave as a demilitarised zone in which there were civilians only? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall any communication from the BH Army in which an answer was provided to you why it was that they were carrying out activities from the demilitarised zones on the basis of the protests that they sent to you, or, rather, that the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska sent to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that they sent to us, but again you showed us a document, an internal BiH Army document, which showed why they were doing this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have in e-court 1D186, please, Bezruchenko's document concerning military developments. It is D55. It's an exhibit now. Page 18 now, please, both in Serbian and in English, paragraph 65. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the last document, 65 ter 0142, a document of the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I meant to tender it once I've shown this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on. Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I forgot to switch on my mike. I am quoting from page 18 in both versions, paragraph 65: "On the BH Army side, anticipating international media attention on Zepa, BH Army Department for Morale was working on the instructions for psychological operations in relation to Zepa. The BiH strategy was to deny presence of BiH Army units in Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde, to attribute military operations to unarmed people, and not to acknowledge any discussions on evacuations. Chief of department, Fikret Muslimovic, sent his suggestions for interviews with foreign journalists to the Zepa leadership: "1. Never mention military units in Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde. "2. Whatever the army is doing in this area, say that it is people. "3. By no means should any evacuation be mentioned."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question based on this is as follows: In your opinion, how much had UNPROFOR contributed to the Muslims implementing what Bezruchenko called the strategy of denial of presence of any BiH units in the safe havens of Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by UNPROFOR contributed to the Muslims implementing this, because it may have been their strategy, but I don't think it worked, because we talked about that again last week. We know for a fact that Bosnian soldiers attacked the Dutch and killed one Dutch at Srebrenica, so they can't deny that they had troops there. The commander of the Bosnian light brigade in Zepa, Avdo Palic, attended discussions early on around Zepa, so they cannot deny that they had troops there. And I don't see how UNPROFOR may have contributed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That was precisely why I showed to you how they had been arming for nearly a year and the quantity of weapons stored in the areas. I wanted to find out whether the UNPROFOR battalions deployed in Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde were aware of these enclaves being armed by way of air-lifts.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, they may have been, but I don't know. Those -- those resupply missions you showed me happened before I got there. And just a clarification here. The UNPROFOR did not have battalions deployed around Zepa and Srebrenica. A battalion is a 500- to 800-man organisation. They had a company, which is an 80- to 120-man organisation, closer to 80 in the case of Zepa, for something about 120 [Realtime transcript read in error "20"] kilometres in circumference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order not to waste time, I'm not going to put to you a document demonstrating that both the BH Army and the UNPROFOR confirmed the crash of a helicopter and that its remnants were found on the location.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would therefore like the Chamber to admit this 65 ter document 0142 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D64.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see in the transcript that some of the figures that I mentioned are not there. I can repeat them, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. If I start again from -- they had a company, which is an 80- to 120-people organisation, closer to 80 people in Zepa. 80, 8-0, to 120. And the enclave I mentioned, 120 kilometres in circumference, and not 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Fortin, can you tell me if the battalion commanders or company commanders, as you said, in Zepa sent any reports to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo pertaining to general mobilisation in Srebrenica that had been declared? We have this document admitted into evidence, and I'm not going to show it to you. Just tell me whether you were aware of that fact or not.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, and probably because it happened before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fortin. This general mobilisation, was it carried out during your term in the command or did that happen afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just said that UNPROFOR may have reported on those things, but I was not aware, because if they knew -- if UNPROFOR knew and reported about it, it happened before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Last week, during the examination, you mentioned seeing a truck loaded with cattle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that when I went down to the village of Zepa on -- it was the 27th of July, in the evening, I saw cattle being loaded on a truck, and trucks loaded with cattle, fridge -- refrigerators, and other such things leaving the village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you didn't switch on your microphone. Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have my mike on now. Can we please see in e-court the Prosecution 65 ter 1D190. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you seen and read this document? Please look at item 3. We don't have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll not be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I have not seen that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we don't have an English translation, I'm going to read item 3, and I'm going to tell the witness that this is an order written by the Command of the Drina Corps. And item 3 reads as follows: "The assistant commander for logistics of the Drina Corps shall, in co-operation with the authorities of Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak and Vlasenica municipalities, and assistants for logistics of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, and the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade, organise the collecting of cattle, establishing proper documents, and registering the number of the cattle thus collected and the transportation thereof ...," to the mentioned farms. Number 4: "Immediately start collecting the cattle as soon as the conditions are created for this job to be conducted in the area of operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Is it common practice that the armies collect cattle or, rather, carcasses in the areas that had been war zones in order to prevent the outbreak of infectious diseases and other health hazard? Was it or is it common practice everywhere in the world?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess it must be prudent to not let animals rot near water sources and things like that, so yes. But in this case, as I mentioned, it was a walking carcass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How long can these walking carcasses survive without human assistance if they are left unattended in a certain area?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, since I was not able to survey the surroundings around the village. And if there was grazing fields or things like that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. We're going to leave other relevant questions once we have eye-witnesses of the events that took place in the enclaves. Thank you for coming here, and thank you for your testimony, and thank you for waiting for the continuation of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Defence, I would like to thank you and the interpreters for making an enormous effort due to the speed of my speech, and I am grateful to the President for his guidance with regard to proper behaviour. On behalf of the Defence, I would like to say that I have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I will not be able to complete it before the recess, but I will complete it certainly before the end of the day and we will be able to start with the next witness, who has been waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have a number of questions for you arising directly out of General Tolimir's cross-examination. I'll start with questions that dealt with the Zepa topic, since that's where we focused on today, but then I want to return to the Srebrenica attack from early July. Last Thursday, General Tolimir focused on certain parts of your OTP witness statement, took you to various pages and paragraphs for some time, and, in particular -- and I just note for the record this was at transcript page 3144. He read from page 22 of your statement, where it refers to a conversation between Ed Joseph and General Tolimir, and I'll just quote it to you again. We don't have to get it up on e-court. And I quote: "On July 22, David Harland informed General Gobillard that Ed Joseph had met Tolimir at Rogatica and spoke with him about the demilitarisation of Zepa under UNPROFOR's supervision, and that Tolimir seemed interested." Do you remember that, the gist of that being put to you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then General Tolimir asked you whether there was any obstruction on the side of the Serbs in terms of, as he put it, this particular matter, referring to the POW exchange discussions. What I first want to do, Colonel, is take a look at the actual report that this passage from your OTP witness statement is based on and refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if we could have 65 ter 2256, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. We have a report. We can see it's dated the 21st of July, 1995. The drafter is David Harland, and, again, can you remind us who David Harland is and what position he held in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, David Harland was at Civil Affairs at sector level, so the same level that General Gobillard and I were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I believe you referred in your Popovic testimony to your reliance and trust in the reports that David Harland would issue and that you reviewed regularly during the course of your duties. Is that -- is that a fair characterisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he usually brought more light on an issue because he had different sources, and he brought the information to us that gave more light to an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we see here that it's being distributed to John Ryan, deputy CAC, UNPROFOR Headquarters Sarajevo. What position is that indicated here, deputy CAC?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Right below that, we have it going to Major-General Gobillard, acting commander of UNPROFOR Headquarters Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in the English, please, and that's page 4 in the B/C/S. And I note that this is one in a series of memoranda that David Harland issued concerning the ongoing negotiations in Zepa. This one, and we can go back to it in a moment, is number 2 in the series.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention here on the second paragraph, where it says: "At around 12.00 noon I received a message from Viktor Bezruchenko and Ed Joseph, who said that they had met with General Tolimir, and that he had indicated some interest in a radical demilitarisation proposal floated by Joseph and myself two days ago." Now, first, is this what was referred to in your witness statement that I cited a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "John Ryan and I," meaning Mr. Harland, "expressed doubts about how sincere the Serbs might be about this, but agreed that Ryan would call Prime Minister Silajdzic today to see whether or not the idea should be pursued." So we have a report that General Tolimir seemed interested, but we have these two UNPROFOR officials expressing doubts about how sincere he might be. Can you share with the Trial Chamber, based on your experience during this time, why those gentlemen harboured that doubt about General Tolimir's sincerity about a demilitarisation plan?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, and that was, I think, the 22nd of July we mentioned, we had been through the events in Srebrenica, and one thing came out clearly then and again later on, that every time we talked to a Serb senior officer, someone from the Main Staff, they were stalling, stalling for time, so they had a plan to reduce the pocket -- the enclave of Srebrenica, they had a plan to take over Zepa. So we now knew that in Srebrenica, every time we talked to a senior Serb officer, he was buying time. In the meantime, they were pursuing their plan, and this created confusion at our level. We did not act as swiftly as we may have, and so they were able to execute their plan. By that time, a few days later, we were doubtful of anything constructive that came from these people, Serb senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. What I want to do next is go directly to a document which General Tolimir showed you today, and that is 1D00163.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I know it's got a P number. I was trying to keep up with them, but I don't know what it is off the top of my head. If somebody can --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit D57.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: D57, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see we have this -- what appears to be some kind of intercepted conversation involving Mr. Amor Masovic that we spent some time on earlier today? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We see here on the first page, first paragraph, the language that you pointed out concerning the lack of participation of one of the VRS members, the details of the agreement not being hammered out. But what I want to turn to with respect to this document is on page 2 of the English, and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir -- just a moment, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Thayer is saying that this document seems or looks like an intercept. This document was introduced by the Prosecution, not by the accused. This is not an intercept. This is a document displaying the way in which communications were exchanged between the Muslims of Zepa with the Muslims in Sarajevo via Paket communications system, and this is what I pointed out in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just, first of all, offer a correction. We did not introduce this document, we did not use this document. This has been used by the Defence. We can see from the "6D102" on the cover, it was used by the Gvero Defence in the last trial. It is not something I'm personally familiar with, but it appears to be some kind of record of a conversation, whatever the means. Be that as it may, if we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it was tendered by Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you look at the ERN number, you can see who introduced this document into the database, whether it was the Defence or the Prosecution, when they disclosed documents to us. It was not us who introduced this document, nor did we assign the ERN number. So please bear that in mind. We received this document from the OTP. We did not introduce it into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You introduced it into evidence, but it was disclosed by the Prosecution to you, to the Defence. I think it's very clear. There's no dispute on that. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the second page of the English, please, if we look at that large paragraph in the middle of the page, Colonel, do you see where it notes that this all-for-all agreement, reached at the airport on 20 July, includes the release of all members of the army from all of the aggressor's prisons, and in this context "aggressor" would mean the Serb prisons and camps, including the new captives from Srebrenica? Now, we can see here that -- well, let me ask you this way: Having seen this passage, do you recall at the time the degree to which accounting for the prisoners who were captured after the fall of Srebrenica became an issue in the negotiations for this all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now. And, of course, with so many men of military age not being accounted for, men coming from Srebrenica who were not accounted for at that time, it became a big issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to quickly go to two other documents, Colonel, that go directly to General Tolimir's question to you as to whether there were any obstructions on the side of the Serbs in terms of this POW exchange all-for-all effort that was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 2076, please. And we'll need to go, I think, to the next page in B/C/S to catch the relevant portion. If you scroll down just a little bit, see if we can pick up -- no, sorry, we have to go to the next page in B/C/S to catch the relevant part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what we have here is another report from David Harland up to John Ryan and General Gobillard. This is dated the 20th of July. And we see, in the first paragraph, that there was a meeting held with representatives of both sides and that an agreement in principle was made. And then the next line states that: "There was no signature, however, because of a dispute about the lists of prisoners taken in the recent Serb attack on Srebrenica." Now, how does this report fit in with your recollection of how things were going at this time, when we had negotiations or meetings going on at the local level with Mr. Torlak, for example, and then we've got meetings going on at the Sarajevo Airport with Mr. Masovic and others at the same time, trying to hammer out this so-called all-for-all agreement? How does this passage here, number 1, square with your recollection of this process?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a full recollection of all of those agreements because, as I mentioned, I was on the move at one point on the 26th of July. I know it was later. But we had spent a few days in HQ UNPROFOR as General Gobillard was acting commander during a few days of the Srebrenica crisis. Then we moved on -- back to sector level. There were many things going in Sarajevo at that time, including the early deployments of the Rapid Reaction Force, so I don't have a clear grasp of this issue. But I remember correctly that those unaccounted for people taken from Srebrenica became a big issue for the Bosnians and made it difficult to reach any kind of agreement on the all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we are running out of time. We must have the second break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have our second break now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to show you one more document on this issue of whether there, in fact, was an all-for-all agreement in place, signed, and whether there was any Serb obstruction during the process of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 1764 on e-court, please. As we can see, we have the third installation in these David Harland Zepa negotiation reports. The subject we can see is: "Zepa Negotiations 3." The date is the 21st of July, and again it's going to John Ryan and to General Gobillard. I'd like to turn to page 2 of the document, please, and this will be page 2 of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the second paragraph, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- where it says: "At about 4.00 p.m., the airport meeting on the exchange of prisoners and the evacuation of Zepa collapsed. The Serbs proposed an all-for-all exchange, but refused to give any names of prisoners taken when they over-ran Srebrenica. Effectively, therefore, the Serbs would not have to release those people taken around Srebrenica. The Bosnians, who claim that there are 6800 people from Srebrenica still unaccounted for, refused to make any agreement without seeing a list of names, or at least a number, of Srebrenica POWs." Now, first, Colonel: By this time, on the 21st of July, can you just generally give the Trial Chamber an idea, did you in Sector Sarajevo have any information concerning the fate or whereabouts of the men who had been in the Srebrenica enclave prior to the VRS taking it over?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly when we started getting reports of what could have happened to those men. Probably around that time. But what we were hearing was that they basically had been killed, especially those men of a military age captured at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, these reports from the Civil Affairs Office, David Harland, I know you're busy during this period of time, but are these the types of reports that would normally come across your desk and that you would rely on in the course of your duties?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would, and I would make sure they got to the General, and he usually had a look at them as soon as they were presented to him, and then made sure they were distributed to his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And having seen this particular document referring to the collapse of the negotiations because of the Serbs' refusal to account for the missing Srebrenica men, does that help you at all in answering General Tolimir's questions to you about, number 1, whether there was, in fact, an all-for-all exchange agreement in place; and, number 2, whether the Serbs obstructed that process?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it definitely does show that there was no agreement -- or the all-for-all exchange agreement alluded to as early as the 20th of July was never reached, and that the Serbs did obstruct because they refused to provide names or whereabouts of the people unaccounted for in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have an objection, because this can pertain to any Serbs except to the Serbs who negotiated about Zepa, General Tolimir and Serbs from Zepa, this is what I focused on, and I did not concern myself with Serbs who were 300 kilometres or more away from me. I didn't have that in mind when I examined the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, is it perhaps a problem of distinction between Serbs and Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the documents speak for themselves, and I'll leave it up to the Trial Chamber, based on the record, as to whether this is even an issue of Serbs from Serbia proper or Bosnian Serbs. And if I may move on, I'm going to try to complete Colonel Fortin's testimony by 1.30 so we can get a head-start on the second witness. I'm not sure that General Tolimir's position is that we are talking about Serbs from Serbia as opposed to Bosnian Serbs. I understood his comment to mean Serbs in Sarajevo conducting negotiations as opposed to Zepa. But I think we can leave it at that. I leave it with the Trial Chamber based on the documents we've seen for the time being. Incidentally, Mr. President, I will not be tendering the documents I've shown to Colonel Fortin at this time. I think we have a sufficient basis, but I can tell you that we will have other witnesses who were directly involved in some of these issues, through whom we will be tendering these exhibits at the appropriate time. So rather than taking up that time now, we'll just keep showing the documents and tender them later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, they discussed here some activities, which did not take place, which I took part in and which are now at issue. However, that wasn't mentioned either in examination-in-chief or in cross-examination. I mentioned documents which had arrived in Zepa which mentioned an all-for-all exchange. Based on that, we could see that the Serbian side did not obstruct anything during negotiations in Zepa. We even allowed for the evacuation to take place of residents and the wounded before the brigade had surrendered. The Serbian side was fully cooperative, so I do not want it to be presented in any other way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are not giving evidence at the moment. You are a party of these proceedings, and I think the Prosecution is dealing with that part of the cross-examination which relates to all-for-all exchange of prisoners of war. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure who can provide me with the clarifications I'm seeking, whether it's Mr. Thayer, the witness, or the accused, but I just want some clarification as to what is an all-for-all agreement in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll start with the man in the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the course of the war, both parties had captured elements -- military personnel from the other side. Now, all-for-all was an exchange -- they were seeking to develop an agreement to exchange all prisoner of wars. What was new at this time was that shortly before, the Serbs had captured many more at Srebrenica when they reduced that -- when they attacked and reduced that enclave, and as mentioned, we were not -- we were starting to hear about the fate of those people that were unaccounted for. But there was a huge number of new prisoner of wars taken by the Serbs that were to be included in that all-for-all exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does that mean all prisoners from both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that was the intent, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I take it that that would be as opposed to a different type of exchange where you might have a one-for-one or a high-value prisoner for a certain amount of prisoners from the other side, just to kind of complete the picture?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to provide a little bit of background or context, if I could, to a number of General Tolimir's questions concerning the series of meetings in Zepa which resulted in an agreement you were shown that was signed on the 24th by Mr. Torlak, the 24th of July, a meeting -- an agreement which was preceded by a meeting on July 19th that you heard about, and an agreement which you were a witness to that was signed by the three local representatives on the 27th of July. So we've got a lot of meetings and agreements that I think were thrown at you one after the other. What I want to do is see if we can get a little sense for the Trial Chamber of what was happening on the ground throughout this period of time, based on what was being reported to you and based on what you saw, personally, when you were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 2438, please. And we need to go to page 26. Okay. I see we don't have a B/C/S translation of this, but I'm only going to be calling your attention to a small portion, and I can read the relevant portions into the record. We have here, on the 22nd of July, another David Harland report to John Ryan and General Gobillard. This is titled "Zepa Negotiations 4." And if we could go to page 3 of this document, please, and that's going to be page 29 in e-court. It would be the prior page, please. There we go. If we could blow up the portion that says "Assessment." David Harland writes in his assessment that: "Our proposal for the total demilitarisation of Zepa remains a long shot. It is true that the Serbs are reluctant to attack the Zepa pocket until they have completely worn down its population. On the other hand, it is hard to imagine that they would accept any arrangement that would leave Zepa in Bosnian hands. I imagine that they will continue to make life in Zepa as miserable as possible for the local population until - demoralised by the assault and abandoned by the international community - they accept the 'evacuation' option being proposed by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, what was the information you were receiving concerning the military activities of the VRS towards the Zepa enclave during this period of time? Let's say starting from shortly after the fall of Srebrenica, 13th, 14th, 15th of July, through this date, the 22nd of July. Can you give the Trial Chamber just a brief idea of, militarily, what were the Serbs doing to the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I don't recall much, except to say that after Srebrenica, Serbs had more forces that they could relocate, so Serb forces closed in on the Zepa enclave, occupying, for example, a large -- a large parking area at the top of the hill where the Ukrainians had their check-point. And I remember the incidents of shelling by the -- by the Bosnian on the Ukrainian command post down in the village. I remember the Serbs blocking the other Ukrainian observation points that were located all around the enclaves, preventing them from going anywhere, but I don't remember any more -- any more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember receiving reports that the Bosnian Serbs were shelling Zepa during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll save some documents I'd show you for another witness on that count. Now, in the course of asking you about whether there was Serb obstruction, General Tolimir showed you an agreement that was signed by Hamdija Torlak on the 24th of July, 1995, signed by him alone, in the presence of Generals Mladic, Tolimir, and Colonel Kusic, the commander of the Rogatica Brigade. He showed you a copy of that agreement. It's 1D107. Now, when he questioned you about this agreement, Colonel, General Tolimir was at great pains to emphasise, and this is at transcript page 3146 -- he went to great pains to emphasise that this agreement on paper provided that the Zepa population would have a free choice of where they could reside. Now, Colonel, you were there when the Muslim population was being removed from that enclave. You saw those people getting taken up out of their village. You said that they came out with nothing. You talked about the looting you saw, not removal of carcasses. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, based on what you saw looking at those people, what choice did they have about where they could reside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer, Witness. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was a very leading question. The Prosecutor says that Tolimir was at great pains, thus giving an indication to the witness that he needs to respond in a way that the Prosecutor expects him to respond. I don't think that leading questions should be put to the witness. The questions should be phrased in such a way as to give no indication to the witness as to who wants to prove what by way of that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd simply ask that the witness be permitted to answer the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this witness is capable to answer, from his recollection, in an appropriate way. Witness, could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, the day I deployed to Zepa, as mentioned earlier, we were stopped in Rogatica, a check-point, a Serb military check-point, Rogatica, for about 18 hours, and we saw there that the evacuation had already started. It was being done using Serb buses and trucks, and I mentioned the truck that we intercepted that was not accompanied by an UNPROFOR soldier like it should have been. All of those vehicles were going to Kladanj, a small city on the Bosnian side of the confrontation line. And from what I could see, there were -- when I arrived in Zepa the next day, people were being removed from where they live, taken up the hill to the parking area at the Ukrainian check-point, where Serb soldiers were showing them into the buses and trucks for evacuation to Kladanj. I don't think that any of them could have opted to stay in Zepa or to go anywhere else in Bosnian-held Bosnia-Herzegovina; not at that point, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe what those people were carrying with them, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. They had their clothes that they were wearing. I saw a couple of women carrying their younger children and trying to catch the four-year-old or the six-year-old that was running around, not really understanding what was going on, with some Serb soldiers prodding them along verbally. One of them was having a good time doing that, from the looks of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I want to turn your attention back to the VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave. General Tolimir claimed repeatedly in his questioning of you last Thursday that the VRS did not attack the UN during its attack on the enclave, and this we can see at transcript 3207 and 3208, if anybody wants a reference. And he put it to you this way: "Was it necessary at all for UNPROFOR to use weapons to counter the Army of Republika Srpska when the Army of Republika Srpska was not attacking UNPROFOR?" And General Tolimir quoted quite liberally from your diary, and I just want to go through a couple of entries in your diary on these precise points that he asked you about in your cross-examination. Before we call it up, I just want to ask you a couple of questions about the diary, itself, and we can do this, I think, in open session. As we can see, some of it was written in French and some of it appears in English. And as we'll look at in a couple of minutes, if you look at the entries from 8 July, say, to 12 July, a number of the entries that were in French not only have dates but have specific times for the entries; 1450 hours, such and such happened; 1500 hours, such and such happened. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber -- or give the Trial Chamber a little bit of background of -- when we're seeing your writing in the diary in French, translated now into English, what were you doing? What did that writing represent? Was that something that was going on at the time, was that something that was going on later? What did you rely on to make those entries in French with those time entries?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, choosing what language to use when I was writing up depended on a number of issues. One, who it was addressed to. Say, if I was writing a report that was to be sent to a higher level, like Headquarters UNPROFOR, I would write it in English. If I was taking notes of a meeting where the interpreter interpreted in English, I would write it in that language. If I was taking notes of a meeting where the interpreter was doing the interpreting in French, I would write in French. And whenever I was personally making notes of events as they occurred, I usually wrote in French because it's my first language.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see that everything is typewritten in your journal. When you were taking these notes originally, were you writing in longhand or were you typing them?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was writing in longhand and usually typing it up at the same night. As soon as we were done moving around visiting -- visiting factions, visiting our own post, or visiting higher headquarters, we would go back to PTT building, where we were headquartered, and I would type it up on a computer right away that same evening. Because I wanted to keep a record of all of those notes, a record that was being shared, when not in a full report, I would discuss with other officers, and then those documents that were in numeric or electronic form already, I just -- when I completed the journal after I returned to home, I just cut-and-paste them into a chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when you were taking these handwritten notes in French, Colonel, first of all, were they contemporaneous with the events that you were recording?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as -- as they were occurring, I always had my notepad with me, so anything that seemed important. And those events, when we were at the headquarters UNPROFOR and my commander was acting commander UNPROFOR, I was recording events as they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were you writing down those notes because you wanted to write a book some day or was there an immediate purpose related to your job for taking down these notes contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I started writing notes right from the start. I decided -- I never held a personal journal in my life, but I decided that this was probably a good opportunity to start something like that. So at first -- and that's at home, on the 1st of May, before leaving -- even going to Bosnia, I started this thing, but my notes were quite sketchy, not a whole lot of personal stuff. But as soon as I arrived and I started attending meetings and taking notes, because my predecessor told me, Every time you go somewhere, note down whatever is being said. He was doing it in point form, summary form, to have a record of what was being done. So he suggested I do that, and I said, Yes, that's a good idea, it can reinforce the idea of a journal. If I'm going to take all of these notes, I might as well make use of them. What I did more, if I can say, is instead of taking notes in point form, I was basically taking everything down and then retyping it at night for ease of access of those records.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may have P585, and this needs to be in private session for the rest of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to, as quickly as I can, take you to some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I have no further questions. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a follow-up question to what constitutes - what was it called all-for-all agreement. In your explanation, you said: "Yes, correct." But then in page 69, 3 to 6, Mr. Thayer clarified with words to the effect that: "Where you might have a one-for-one or a high-value prisoner for -- a certain amount of prisoners from the other side, just to kind of complete the picture." Now, I'm not yet clear what exactly this agreement would be about. Would it be about one prisoner for one prisoner or many prisoners for a high-value prisoners, or both?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, what -- I believe what Mr. Thayer was saying is that in many cases there could have been punctual negotiations for the exchange of one, two, or a few prisoners following a fire-fight, for example, following for some specific incident. In that particular case, with the insistence of the UN, both parties were trying to achieve an agreement to exchange all the prisoners that they held at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have another question for you. On the 24th, last week, you told us something about the able-bodied men who had disappeared from Srebrenica. It is page 3144, I quote: "If you look at the bigger picture not long before the other enclave of Srebrenica had been evacuated with no UN supervision, and we know that many thousands of men disappeared, never to be seen again." Today you were asked, and this is on page 66, line 20 of today's transcript -- no, it's page 65, line 20 and the following, and you said: "I'm not sure exactly when we started getting reports of what could have happened to those men. Probably around that time. But what we were hearing was that they basically had been killed, especially those men of military age captured at Srebrenica." These two portions of your evidence were related to the same events in Srebrenica and your experience with these occurrences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you get at that time some more information about the fate of these missing people?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly when I learned about that, but I know that quite early after Srebrenica we had reports that some people of military age had tried to escape from Srebrenica and had been caught in fire-fights with the Serbs and were killed. Others were evacuated with the rest of the population, but because they were military age, they were segregated and eventually disposed of. So quite early after the events at Srebrenica, we started having that kind of information, but exactly when, I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, this concludes the questioning for you. The Chamber has to thank you for your attendance and your patience to be here last week and today again. Thank you very much again, and now you are free to return to your official post in Western Africa. Thank you again for coming here to The Hague again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think there are only four minutes left. It seems not to be a very good idea to start with the next witness right now. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think you're correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, we should adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
